title: Never break faith
hook: value nothing that makes you break your word or lose self-respect (Meditations 3.7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: if you find anything better. Your line was nothing better. Which of the four, justice, truth, self-control or courage, got crowded out of your day? Day five hundred forty-three.

Curtains can tell you something about a house. Some hang there for warmth, or for sleep. And sometimes a curtain is there for another reason: the purchase nobody mentioned, the deleted message, the plan someone would rather nobody saw. Marcus Aurelius used curtains as a test. In the seventh entry of his third book, he lists the things a person should never count as worth having, and he ends the list with an image of walls and curtains. Today: never break faith.
screen: `CURTAINS ON A HOUSE.` → `WHAT NEEDS CURTAINS?` → `NEVER BREAK FAITH.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Never value anything as good for you, Marcus writes, if it will one day force you to break your word or lose your self-respect. Notice the order. He doesn't start with what's forbidden. He starts with what we value. If a thing would cost you your word, it was never really a gain. Second, the longer list. He goes on: nothing that makes you hate anyone, suspect anyone, curse anyone, play the hypocrite. Each one is a small way of breaking faith, with another person or with yourself. Third, walls and curtains. The list ends with anything you'd want that needs walls and curtains around it. It's a plain household test. If a desire only works in hiding, Marcus counts it as a loss, however good it looks. It connects to the line from two days ago: think only what you could say out loud. Fourth, the person who keeps faith. Marcus describes them. They put their own mind and its goodness first. They don't make a tragedy of things, don't groan, don't need either solitude or a crowd. They don't chase life and they don't run from it. Here's the useful part for an ordinary day. Breaking faith is rarely one big betrayal. It's usually small: the call you said you'd make, the favor you said you'd do, the time you said you'd be there. A small promise kept is still a promise kept, and a word that holds in small things is easier to trust in large ones. That's what Marcus is protecting: not a reputation, but a self you can respect.
screen: `NEVER COUNT IT A GAIN IF IT COSTS YOUR WORD.` · `NO HATE, SUSPICION, CURSES, HYPOCRISY.` · `NOTHING THAT NEEDS WALLS AND CURTAINS.` · `THE ONE WHO KEEPS FAITH.` · then, large: `KEEP FAITH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one promise you've made that's still open. It can be tiny: I'll call you back, I'll send that, I'll be there at six. Picture the person who heard you say it. Now picture keeping it today, plainly, without fuss. Decide when. Then let the breath carry a quiet sense of what it's like to be someone whose word holds. The bell holds the time.
Never break faith. Marcus's rule: value nothing that would make you break your word, lose your self-respect, or want what needs walls and curtains. Today's word.
Your line: keep faith. Keep one promise today, even a small one, and keep it on time. Day five hundred forty-three.

screen: `DAY 543 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HONOR THE POWER OF JUDGMENT.`

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius treat Meditations 3.7 as a household test: if a desire only works in hiding, behind walls and curtains, they count it as a loss.

pairs: neither chases life nor runs from it
usually small, not one big betrayal

myth: Marcus starts with a list of forbidden acts
he starts with what we value: never count as a gain what costs your word.
Marcus counts hating and suspecting as ways to break faith
they're on his list beside cursing and playing the hypocrite.
Marcus says the faithful person needs solitude
he says they need neither solitude nor a crowd.

fork.setup: a coworker offers to cover for you if you skip the meeting you promised to lead. nobody would know. what fits 3.7?
options: keep the promise and lead the meeting.
skip it, but tell yourself it's fine.
fork.reveal: Marcus counts nothing a gain that costs your word, and a plan that needs hiding fails his walls-and-curtains test.

original.note: Greek, 'faith, trust, a pledge': the word for the faith Marcus says never to break.

trapdoor: what it means: value nothing that costs your word, your self-respect, or needs to stay hidden.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's list runs from broken promises to wanting 'walls and curtains', a picture of private vice from a very public man.

notes: 3.7 paraphrased: never value as profitable what compels you to break your promise, lose self-respect, hate, suspect, curse, act the hypocrite, or desire anything needing walls and curtains (Long's wording, from memory). Confirm.
The description of the person who keeps faith (no tragedy-acting, no groaning, needs neither solitude nor many people, neither pursues nor flies from life) is from the remainder of 3.7; confirm.
Greek pistis: confirm that 3.7 uses 'pistin parabenai' (break faith).
